lesson.grammar_point: reported speech and reporting verbs in regulatory communication

listenings.text: The federal transport agency moved this afternoon to calm investors after a week of speculation about toll road contracts. In a statement, the agency confirmed that the tariff review for highway concessions will go ahead in October, but clarified that it would follow the formula written into each contract. The agency's director acknowledged that seven operators had filed rebalancing claims after the floods, and said the claims would be assessed individually. She declined to say whether the floods would be treated as force majeure. Market reaction was cautious. One analyst told us that investors had expected a clearer answer on the floods, and warned that uncertainty over the claims could delay two auctions planned for the first half of next year.

Most investors read the tariff clause and the investment schedule, and then they stop. I want to talk about the two clauses they skip. The first is force majeure. People think it is a formality, but in a country with floods and droughts it decides who pays when the road is under water. Read the list of events, and read who has to prove what. The second is the grandfathering clause. When a government changes the rules, this is the sentence that says whether your contract is protected or not. I have seen a fund lose a year of returns because its lawyers assumed the old rules would continue, and the clause said otherwise. None of this is exciting. All of it belongs in your due diligence.

paras: By the time yesterday’s press conference ended, three different headlines were already circulating. One said the government would cut toll road tariffs. Another said the concessions would be renegotiated. A third said nothing would change. All three came from the same forty minutes, and none of them was exactly what the agency said.

The director opened by confirming that the tariff review for the third batch of highways would begin in October, after a public consultation of forty-five days. That part was a decision. She then indicated that the review could lead to lower tariffs on some stretches of road, which is a signal, not a promise. When a journalist asked whether contracts would be renegotiated, she clarified that the review followed the formula already written in each contract, and that operators were not expected to cut investment during the consultation period.

The more important news came in answer to a question about the floods in the south. The director acknowledged that several operators had filed rebalancing claims, and said that each claim would be assessed case by case. She did not say whether the floods would be treated as force majeure, and a senior official later suggested that the agency had not yet reached a view. She also confirmed that contracts signed before 2025 are protected by a grandfathering clause, which means the new rules do not apply to them.

For investors doing due diligence, the useful lesson is not the headline. It is the verbs. Confirmed means you can build a model on it. Indicated and suggested mean you should build two. And when a statement is reported without a person — the operator is said to be preparing a claim — it means somebody wanted the information out without having to own it.

items.situation: A fund manager asks what the agency decided yesterday. Report the one decision, without making it stronger.
tips: The director confirmed that the tariff review would begin in October, after a forty-five-day public consultation.
Confirmed for the decision; would begin, one step back in time.

items.situation: The same manager asks whether tariffs will fall. Report the signal as a signal.
tips: She indicated that tariffs could fall on some stretches, but that was a signal, not a promise.
Indicated, not confirmed. Could, not will.

items.situation: An investor says he heard all concessions will be renegotiated. Correct him politely.
tips: That is not what was said. The agency clarified that the review follows the formula already in each contract.
Clarified is the verb for correcting a misunderstanding.

items.situation: Explain to a CFO from Singapore what a grandfathering clause means for her contract signed in 2023.
tips: Her contract is protected by a grandfathering clause, so the new rules do not apply to it.

items.situation: Report a rumor you cannot confirm about an operator preparing a large claim.
tips: The operator is said to be preparing a rebalancing claim, but nobody has confirmed it.
is said to + be + -ing for something happening now.

items.situation: A lender asks what happens if the operator fails to invest for two years.
tips: That would be a material breach, and the lenders could use their step-in right to replace the operator.
Material breach first, then the consequence.
